metadata.code_evidence: SECRET_KEY = 'lr66%-a!$km5ed@n5ug!tya5bv!0(yqwa1tn!q%0%3m2nh%oml'
metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: literal assignment in pygoat/settings.py; no environment variable override is provided in the file. Deployment-dependent: impact requires that the deployment keeps this key (the shipped Dockerfile/docker-compose do).
metadata.data_flow: known SECRET_KEY -> forge Django session cookies / signed values -> act as any account (including staff/admin) in the deployment.

extra.message: Authentication bypass in the OTP login: the POST verification accepts the administrator record whenever its stored OTP matches, independently of the e-mail address in the cookie ('or otp.objects.filter(id=2,otp=otpR)'). The administrator OTP is a three digit number, so it can be guessed within a few hundred requests and the attacker is then logged in as the administrator.

metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: the second disjunct matches the fixed administrator row without comparing the e-mail, and no rate limiting/lockout exists on the endpoint (it is @csrf_exempt and requires no session). Deployment-dependent: the administrator OTP row (id=2) must exist in the database, which the lab data provides.
metadata.data_flow: request.POST['otp'] + request.COOKIES['email'] -> boolean check at introduction/views.py:514 -> 'Login Success as user' page rendered for the attacker without proving ownership of the administrator mailbox.

extra.message: State changing operation without CSRF protection: the money transfer endpoint performs the balance change on a plain GET request and the authentication decorator is commented out ('# @authentication_decorator'), so a third-party site can make an authenticated victim's browser trigger the transfer (the cookie auth_cookiee is attached automatically), and no CSRF token is validated.

metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: GET-based state change, no CSRF token check, no authentication decorator in the source. Deployment-dependent: the victim must have a valid auth_cookiee cookie, and the hard-coded JWT secret (finding-026) also allows forging that cookie directly.
metadata.data_flow: cross-site GET request to /mitre/9/lab/api/<recipent>/<amount> with the victim's auth_cookiee cookie -> jwt.decode at introduction/mitre.py:194 -> recipent.balance += amount / User[0].balance -= amount (introduction/mitre.py:203-207).

extra.message: Access control based on a spoofable request header: the ssrf_target view decides whether the caller is 'local' by inspecting the X-Forwarded-For header, which any client can set, so the intended restriction (only loopback clients may access the target page) can be bypassed by sending a forged header.

metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: the header value is trusted without validation and used for the authorization decision. Deployment-dependent: whether the deployment strips/normalises X-Forwarded-For (no trusted-proxy configuration is present in the settings).
metadata.data_flow: request header X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1 -> introduction/views.py:943-948 -> ip == '127.0.0.1' check at introduction/views.py:950 -> access to Lab/ssrf/ssrf_target.html.

extra.message: Missing authentication on a sensitive data endpoint: the view exposes the credit card number, social security number and API key of every registered user as JSON without any authentication or authorization check (the code comments state this explicitly). Any unauthenticated client can harvest all users' personal data and API keys.

metadata.code_evidence:
def all_users_data_view(request):
    # MAJOR SECURITY FLAW: This endpoint allows ANY user (even unauthenticated ones!)
    # to see ALL users' sensitive data!
    # This demonstrates why proper authentication/authorization is essential.
    
    # Note for students: Notice how there are no checks for who's requesting the data!

    all_users_data = []
    for user_data in UserData.objects.all():
        all_users_data.append({
            'username': user_data.user.username,
            'credit_card': user_data.credit_card,  # Completely exposed! No masking!
            'ssn': user_data.ssn,  # Sending full SSN - terrible practice!
            'api_key': user_data.api_key  # API keys should never be exposed like this
        })
    
    # In a secure application, we would add:
    # if not request.user.is_authenticated or not request.user.is_staff:
    #     return JsonResponse({'error': 'Unauthorized'}, status=401)
    
    return JsonResponse({'users': all_users_data})
metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: the view has no @login_required and performs no permission check before serialising UserData.objects.all(). Deployment-dependent: the lab container must be reachable (docker-compose exposes port 8000).
metadata.data_flow: unauthenticated GET to the all-users endpoint -> dataexposure/views.py:112-132 -> UserData.objects.all() -> JsonResponse with username, credit_card, ssn and api_key of every user.

extra.message: Forgable session token: the session cookie is only base64(username:timestamp) with no signature, HMAC or server-side state, so an attacker can craft base64('admin:<any timestamp>') and is accepted as the administrator account with access to the dashboard and the admin e-mail.

metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: the dashboard only decodes the cookie and takes the username part; no integrity check exists. Deployment-dependent: the lab container must be reachable (port 5000).
metadata.data_flow: attacker crafted cookie 'session' = base64('admin:2024-01-01 00:00:00') -> app.py:111 username = base64.b64decode(session_token).decode().split(':')[0] -> users[username]['role'] used to render the dashboard.

extra.message: Weak password reset mechanism: the reset token is md5(email:timestamp), i.e. derived from public data with second precision and no random component, and the token is disclosed directly in the HTTP response ('Password reset link: /reset/<token>') to whoever requested the reset for that e-mail address. An attacker can therefore request a reset for another user's e-mail address and immediately obtain the token to take over that account.

metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: token generation at app.py:86 and disclosure in the flashed message at app.py:90. Deployment-dependent: the target account's e-mail must be known (the lab stores them in the users dictionary).
metadata.data_flow: POST /reset-password with the victim's e-mail -> token = hashlib.md5(f'{email}:{datetime.now()}').hexdigest() at app.py:86 -> flash(f'Password reset link: /reset/{token}') at app.py:90 -> GET /reset/<token> renders the reset form.

extra.message: Hard-coded Flask session secret: app.secret_key is the literal 'your-secret-key-here'. All Flask session cookies are signed with this publicly known value, so an attacker can forge arbitrary session cookies (including admin sessions) for this application.

metadata.code_evidence:
app = Flask(__name__)
app.secret_key = 'your-secret-key-here'  # Vulnerable: Hardcoded secret key
metadata.preconditions: Source-confirmed: literal assignment in the source; the Dockerfile/docker-compose start the app with this file unmodified. Deployment-dependent: the lab container must be reachable.
metadata.data_flow: known secret 'your-secret-key-here' -> forge Flask session cookie -> authenticated access to the lab without knowing the credentials.

extra.message: The Flask development server is started with debug=True on 0.0.0.0:5000. The interactive Werkzeug debugger console is then exposed, which allows arbitrary code execution by anyone who can reach the port when an exception is triggered.

if __name__ == '__main__':

metadata.data_flow: any request triggering an exception in the Flask app -> Werkzeug interactive debugger with console -> arbitrary Python execution.

extra.message: Authentication cookie issued without the Secure attribute: the session identity cookie 'userid' (and the identical cookies issued at introduction/views.py:305 and 319) is set with secure=False and samesite=None, and is valid for roughly one year (max_age=31449600). Over plain HTTP or through any SSL-stripping position the cookie, which is the only credential used by the AUTH lab login flow, is transmitted in clear text and can be replayed to impersonate the user.

extra.message: Security decision based on a client supplied header: the 'secret' view returns the secret key S3CR37K3Y to any request whose X-Host header equals 'admin.localhost:8000'. The header is entirely attacker controlled, so the protection can be bypassed trivially.
